A Shadow Can Outrun Light

physics 21 Aug 2026

Sentence31 words · 0.2 min

The Moon’s shadow on the cloud tops, from the ISS, 2017. NASA.

A shadow’s edge is not a thing but a place where something is absent — and a place can outrun light: a swept laser crosses the Moon at eight times c.

Earth’s shadow tracking across the Moon, October 2023. Its edge sweeps at over 3,000 km/s.

The speed limit in relativity is not a limit on speeds. It is a limit on carriers — on anything that moves energy, matter or a message. A shadow is none of those. Stand a finger in front of a lamp: move it a centimetre and the shadow on the wall moves ten. Put the wall further off and the same centimetre moves the shadow a kilometre. Nothing had to be accelerated. The shadow is only a statement about which parts of the wall are receiving photons, and a statement can be rewritten as fast as you please.

Put numbers on it. The Moon is 384,400 km away. Turn a laser on its mount once a second and the beam sweeps 2π radians in that second, so the spot crosses the lunar surface at about 2.4 billion metres per second — some eight times the speed of light. Every photon in the beam still travels at exactly c, and takes 1.28 seconds to arrive. What exceeds c is the arrival point, and that point is made of different photons at every instant.

That is why causality survives. An astronaut at crater A cannot signal a colleague at crater B with the passing spot: whether and when it reaches B was fixed at the laser, 1.28 seconds earlier, and nothing done at A can reach B in time to change it. No influence runs along the ground. The spot is a row of unrelated events we read as motion — the same trick as bulbs flashing in turn on a theatre sign, where the light appears to run and no light runs anywhere. Relativity forbids the transport of a cause. It says nothing about the speed of a coincidence.

The claim

Point a laser at the Moon and turn it on its mount at one revolution per second. The Moon is 384,400 kilometres away, the beam sweeps through 2π radians in that second, and the bright spot therefore crosses the lunar surface at about 2.4 billion metres per second — some eight times the speed of light. The arithmetic is not in dispute and the physics is not violated. Nor is this a special property of lasers: the shadow of your finger, thrown from a lamp onto a wall a long way off, races along the wall as fast as the geometry demands, and the edge of the Earth’s own shadow sweeps across the Moon during an eclipse at more than 3,000 kilometres per second.

A shadow is a place, not a thing: here the Moon’s, laid on the Earth.

The reason none of this is forbidden is that a spot of light, or the edge of a shadow, is not a thing. It is a statement about which parts of a distant surface happen to be receiving photons and which are not. The photons themselves each travel outward at exactly c and take 1.28 seconds to reach the Moon, and no two of them are ever the same photon. What moves quickly is the arrival point, and the arrival point is a different set of photons at every instant, each of which left the laser at its own moment along its own straight line.

Two kinds of speed

It is worth naming the distinction plainly, because almost every apparent violation of the light-speed limit turns on it. Some speeds belong to a carrier: an electron, a photon, a sound wave, a push travelling down a rod. Others belong to a pattern: the crest of a wave, the point where two lines cross, the edge of a shadow, the bright spot where a beam meets a surface. A carrier is a thing that is here and then there. It must be accelerated, it carries energy, and it obeys the limit. A pattern is a statement about the arrangement of many separate things, and moving it costs nothing at all, because nothing is being moved.

Once you look for it, the distinction is everywhere. The Mexican wave in a stadium travels far faster than any spectator moves. The dark band that runs backwards down a queue of braking cars is not a thing. The terminator on the Earth — the line between day and night — sweeps across the equator at about 465 metres per second, and it is not travelling anywhere; it is the edge of an illumination.

One shadow, sampled through an eclipse. Nothing crossed the Moon; the lit region changed.

The scissors

The textbook example is a pair of very long, very sharp scissors, closing. Two straight blades meeting at a small angle θ have an intersection point, and if one blade closes with speed v, the intersection runs outward along the blades at roughly v divided by tan θ. Make the angle small enough and the arithmetic gives any speed you want, including superluminal ones. The point of intersection is a pattern: it is where two edges happen to coincide, and coincidences are free.

The objection people raise is instructive, because it is right about the physics and wrong about the conclusion. Real blades are not rigid. Push one end of a steel blade and the far end does not move at once: the push travels as a compression wave at the speed of sound in steel, about 5 kilometres per second, a millionth of c. So you cannot cause the far intersection by squeezing the handles. Relativity goes further, and says a perfectly rigid body cannot exist at all, precisely because it would transmit a push instantaneously.

None of that rescues subluminality, because the superluminal intersection was never caused by the squeeze. It was arranged in advance by the geometry — the blades already lined up, already closing — and the crossing point runs along a track laid before the experiment began. Superluminal patterns are always like this: set up beforehand, never steered from inside.

Why the limit is about causes

Relativity’s real objection to superluminal signalling is not that fast things are unseemly. It is that “faster than light” is not a frame-independent statement about time order. If two events are separated by more distance than light can cross in the time between them, then observers moving at different velocities disagree about which came first — this is the relativity of simultaneity, and it is not an illusion of measurement but a fact about the geometry of spacetime. So a signal that outran light in one frame would, in some other perfectly ordinary frame, arrive before it was sent. Chain two such signals in opposite directions and you can arrange a reply that precedes the question — the “tachyonic antitelephone” that Benford, Book and Newcomb set out in 1970.

That is the whole content of the limit. Not nothing moves faster than c, but no cause reaches its effect faster than c. Test the laser spot against it directly. An astronaut at crater A cannot use the passing spot to signal a colleague at crater B, because whether and when the spot arrives at B was fixed at the laser more than a second earlier, and nothing done at A can reach B in time to change it. No influence runs along the ground from A to B. The spot is a sequence of unrelated events that we read as motion, exactly as a row of bulbs flashing in turn on a theatre sign produces a light that appears to run along the sign while no light runs anywhere.

The careful version: front velocity

Physics has had to be precise about this, because dispersive media make the question genuinely subtle. Léon Brillouin, building on Arnold Sommerfeld’s work between about 1907 and 1914, distinguished five velocities a wave can be said to have: phase, group, energy transport, signal and front. They come apart routinely. Inside a hollow metal waveguide the phase velocity exceeds c as a matter of ordinary engineering, and nobody is troubled.

In a medium with anomalous dispersion the group velocity can exceed c, go infinite, or turn negative. In a striking experiment by Wang, Kuzmich and Dogariu in 2000, a pulse through a caesium vapour cell had a group velocity of −c/310: the peak of the outgoing pulse left the far side of the cell before the peak of the incoming pulse reached the near side. Tunnelling does something similar — the Hartman effect, from 1962, has the traversal time of a barrier stop growing once the barrier is thick enough, which makes the apparent speed unbounded.

None of these transmits information faster than light, and the reason is always the front. The leading edge of a pulse — the first, faint, discontinuous onset of a signal that was absent before — travels at exactly c in every medium, without exception. What the exotic media do is reshape the part of the pulse that comes after the front, amplifying its leading flank and attenuating its trailing one until the peak appears to have arrived early. The peak was never the message. Everything the receiver learns, it learns from the front, and the front is punctual.

Out in the sky

Nature runs these effects at scale. Quasar jets show apparent transverse motion of up to ten times c; Martin Rees explained it in 1966 as projection — material moving at very nearly light speed, almost along the line of sight, nearly keeps pace with its own emitted light, so a long journey appears to happen in a short time. Light echoes do the same for dust: the ring around V838 Monocerotis seemed to swell superluminally, because we were watching an expanding sphere of light illuminate successively more distant dust, not any material expansion at all.

The most physical case is a pulsar. A neutron star’s magnetic field co-rotates with it, but the co-rotation cannot continue beyond the radius where a rigidly turning pattern would have to move at c — the light cylinder, about 1,600 kilometres out for the Crab pulsar’s 33-millisecond period. Outside that radius the field cannot co-rotate, so it is torn open into a wind. Here the impossibility of superluminal carriers sets a real, structural boundary in a real object, while the beam’s own sweep, out at interstellar distances, is a pattern and races along as fast as the geometry likes.

Two familiar things should be set aside as different questions entirely.

  • Cherenkov radiation — the blue glow in a reactor pool — comes from particles genuinely outrunning light, but light in water, whose phase velocity is only about three-quarters of c.
  • Cosmological recession: distant galaxies recede faster than light without moving through space at all. Expansion adds distance between things, and relativity’s limit is a local statement, about what passes what.

What is actually forbidden

So the rule survives every one of these, unamended, because it was never the rule people take it for. Energy cannot be transported faster than light. Matter cannot. A signal cannot. Cause cannot reach effect faster than light.

Everything else — the shadow racing along the wall, the crossing point of the blades, the spot on the Moon, the peak of a pulse in caesium vapour, the searchlight sweep of a pulsar’s beam across a nebula — is a pattern. Patterns are not exempt from the speed limit. They were simply never subject to it, because a place where something is absent is not going anywhere.
